utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case Number IT-02-60-T, The Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, although as I went out of the courtroom, I felt a little unwell. And because of that, I would like to point out to some omissions that I recalled after I finished my testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean by some omissions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday in the course of my testimony, I was supposed to give testimony as a protected witness. That did not happen. And in the course of my testimony yesterday, I was not sure and occasionally I was a little scared. I didn't know whether I was a protected witness or not. But at the end, when you said that the witness should be taken out, I then turned around, and then I saw the journalists, reporters, the media, which means that I was not protected. That was an omission of this institution which brought me, my family, in a very unpleasant situation after my testimony. And I wouldn't want my family to be at any risk for the -- for the Srebrenica -- from July 1995 to happen again, particularly not to my daughter who is 6 years old. Now what I want this Tribunal to tell me is whether I am under threat, whether I am at risk or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, first of all, I have to apologise to you for this omission. I think this Trial Chamber did not care enough to make sure the status of your testimony. Secondly, I would like to say that we'll finish your cross-examination today and hope to send you back as soon as possible. At this moment, I haven't seen any damage, substantial damage, done to you at this moment. Maybe the impact will be felt later on but anyway, we will bear that in mind to see if there's any remedies in that aspect. Are you ready to proceed, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Any cross-examination? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before coming to testify yesterday, I take it you met with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, Your Honour microphone, please. We cannot hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I do have it on, Your Honour. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have a slight cold. I'll try to shout a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before coming here to testify, you met with the Prosecution, did you not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one of the reasons for meeting with them was to go over your testimony for this particular trial. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's one reason. But there are many reasons why I wanted to see the Prosecutor beforehand regarding the security implications and possible consequences for me and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. But one of the purposes for meeting with the Prosecution was to also for him to walk you through your testimony yesterday and here today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, I did not need to have that meeting for that purpose, to recall what happened in July 1995. That's deeply buried in my heart, in my memory, and I still remember a lot of details from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Well, let's go through some of the events, then. And I want to start with -- I will start with as early as 1992, if that's okay with you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You went to Srebrenica in July, I believe it was 22nd, 23rd of 1992, not as a refugee but for the purpose of fighting or organising a resistance. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I came when -- I arrived one week later to Srebrenica, not to organise resistance because it was already organised, but to join it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you didn't go there as a refugee, you went there as a resistance fighter?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To join the resistance, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you had already been involved in the resistance in Tuzla. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly, just preserving some lines, positions, without any offensive operations on either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you were a commander, were you not, of a particular unit?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What were you a commander of?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of one artillery weapon which has a crew of up to five soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so when you went to Srebrenica back in July 22nd, 23rd, as you indicated, the resistance had already begun and Naser Oric was in command, was he not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you know Naser Oric quite well, do you not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I knew him only slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My question wasn't whether you knew him then quite slightly. I asked that you know him very well. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that even now I know him well, his psychological state, his intentions, but I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But you fought with him, did you not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With units, not with Naser. With the units who were resisting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And those units were under Naser Oric, right?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One of the missions for those units was to go and raid Serb villages, was it not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the objective. The purpose was to resist the units of the VRS and of the Yugoslav army that were attacking on a daily basis and were expelling Bosniaks from those areas. Sir, we had to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you saying here today, Mr. Mandzic, that you did not participate or Naser Oric did not participate in attacking Serb villages, burning down Serb houses, killing Serbs in that area?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, that's a two-part question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, that was a compound question and an important compound question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, Your Honour. I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, put your question another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And by the way, I think I have to remind both parties and the witness, if the witness feels there's some questions that are difficult to answer and it's very sensitive, you could ask the Chamber to go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can have it in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During the period of 1992/1993, when you were fighting for or under or at the direction of Naser Oric, one of the objectives was to attack Serb villages and gather war booty, isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was to liberate the villages, to resist ethnic cleansing -- to resist the VRS units and the Yugoslav army and to get hold of food and equipment, et cetera, and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say get hold of food, you're talking about getting hold of it from Serb villagers, are you not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was food in the liberated Muslim villages because the food was mostly in the Muslim villages because Muslims were a predominant population in those villages and the entire municipality of Srebrenica and Bratunac and the neighbouring municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it's your testimony here today that you did not attack -- you or Naser Oric and his units did not attack any Serb villages. That's your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most important objective was to liberate the Bosniak villages, but during those operations there were some attacks on Serb villages, or rather, I'm sorry, Serb units -- on Serb units, because Serb units shelled and attacked on a daily basis Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review Mr. Oric's indictment? He's currently against the United Nations Detention Unit here thanks to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I ask, what unit were you with when you were fighting with Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a unit. It was Biljeg Battalion, but I have to reiterate I was not in any way joining in any operations with Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you aware that that particular battalion is mentioned in the indictment against Mr. Oric for atrocities committed on civilian Serbs during the period when you, in fact, were serving under Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I'm not aware of that. I have to say that that unit that I was in, its purpose was to liberate Bosniak villages and to provide supplies for the soldiers and the civilians who were with us, I mean mostly food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were injured, I believe you've indicated, sometime around the end of January 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could get some water from the usher because we don't have any water here. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you continued to -- your military service didn't end at that point. You continued shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a short while, until the demilitarisation on the 18th of April, or generally in April. I can't quite recall when the day was, when the demilitarisation occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday, you indicated -- you were asked a question about demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you were asked a similar question the first time you testified.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on both occasions, and correct me if I am wrong, you had indicated that indeed Srebrenica had been demilitarised, and that the few weapons that were there were more or less, at least yesterday's testimony, was that they were trophy weapons, a few citizens had weapons because of security purposes.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, three and a half years ago regarding my testimony in court and recalling my testimony yesterday, all heavy weapons were handed over to UNPROFOR, tank weapons, anti-tank, AA weapons, and it was obvious that they were handed over. I know about the handover of some automatic, semi automatic guns. But on the other hand, I presume that most of the people who had hunting rifles or pistols for which they had their permits in the previous system, they had kept that, and I said that and I'm saying that now, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were hundreds of people like that because the town had nearly 40.000 people in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was Naser Oric still around?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of course he was. By that point, he had been decorated, and he was a brigadier, was he not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. He said ages ago that he got the rank of a general in the month of June in 1992, so that's not true. So what you're saying about him getting the rank of brigadier, I don't know whether it's true, but I know that he was -- he was already a general in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm getting it from the Prosecution's indictment against Mr. Oric where it also states that during that period of Srebrenica, the fall of Srebrenica, the 28th division was actively operating in that vicinity. So my question to you, sir, was the 28th division operating at that time in and around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the operations that you're stating here, in around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, in the period of the demilitarisation. I presume you're asking me about that particular period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So let me get this straight --

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But on the other hand, if you allow me, I do recall that there were people leaving the demilitarised zone, people who were hungry, who were barefoot, who went to their own houses to find some food and so on. And most of those people who left the zone, VRS army captured them, detained them, and most of them never returned. They were never seen again. And I'm quoting the example from some of the groups, one of the group contained 60 people in April 1994 they went to Zepa to get some food. And many people, 10 to 15, disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, could I ask you what's the relevance of these questions? I understand that you have the right to ask some questions to attack the credibility of this witness. But it seems to me that the questions you asked is a little bit far away from the subject matter of the testimony of this witness. I hope you could not drag on along this line and come back to the subject, the main subject, of the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may briefly for the Court's convenience, the gentleman seems -- insists that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to these long dialogues in front of the witness. They may have a detrimental impact on the witness. I've seen how it was done in front of Mr. Ruez, which we did not object to but I think at this point, if Mr. Karnavas has something serious to say, he should say it out of the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you may continue asking questions of this witness, but bear in mind do not drag along for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me put the question back to you. Is it your testimony here today that Naser Oric was not operating in and out of Srebrenica as the commander of various units including the 28th division, which is how it was renamed at the end, during this period, from 1993 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I can say that now in half an hour, you have been linking the question and the case of Naser Oric with my testimony. And this question, too, whether there were operations or whether there were no operations that you're talking about, I don't know. From April 1993 until the fall of Srebrenica in June 1995, I was mostly devoted to my rehabilitation, because I had been wounded and I had many problems. And later on, I was bringing up my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you also devoted to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' correction, I was worrying about the children in secondary school.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just tell you something else. If you want the full truth, the commander that you're talking about, the commander of Srebrenica, from April 1992 until this date, I'm not in a good relationship with him. That doesn't mean that I'm either going to attack him or defend him. I think he can defend himself, if he can't, he's going to take lawyers. That's the truth. I think that in that report you see before him, I think that's what I stated. We are not friends. That doesn't mean that I'm going to defend him here or attack him, and I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were also involved in SDA politics, were you not, during this period?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that party was banned in Srebrenica throughout the war. I mentioned that or perhaps you're not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do see where you've talked about it. Now, the SDA is the -- who was the leader of the SDA during that period?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't even confirm that. Several people changed, and I think that several candidates who were there never received the confirmation from the higher committee or from the presidency of that party that you're mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you cannot tell us today who was the head of the SDA when you were actively involved in it during those periods of times prior to the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If names mean anything to you, the person who was there until April 1992 was the president, Efendic Hamed. He was killed in July 1995 in Srebrenica. From 1993 to 1995, there was a rivalry, whether it would be Hamed or somebody else, and some other people imposed themselves, so there were several candidates, but nobody got the confirmation or the appointment from the presidency of the BH, but I don't know what this is in any connection with my testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did the party exist at the presidency level?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, on the level of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in other municipalities under the control of the army of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who was the head of the SDA party throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, so he was the president of a party that he banned throughout the war. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I thought you said earlier that the party was banned throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My objection is relevance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'd be happy to address the relevancy issue, Your Honour. The gentleman claims not to know what's going on in Srebrenica prior to the fall of Srebrenica. The issue of the 28th division is a critical issue because of their strength. The Prosecution has documents which we have from the UN that outline the strength of the 28th division which was much higher than the Drina Corps itself. I find it kind of incredible that someone involved in SDA politics where Mr. Izetbegovic's own party is involved was living in a small area in an enclave where they're going out and they're committing atrocities and he seems to be totally unaware of it. At one point, you had cautioned me about the tu quoque principle. I fully understand that. But part of the theory of the Defence is that the 28th division was a highly motivated and resourceful army. And during the period at one point when they left Srebrenica, there was concern by the corps and by various units of the corps as to the strength and the ability to wreak havoc, perhaps even taken Zvornik. So that's the purpose of my question, Your Honour. Also, the gentleman has insisted throughout and yesterday was a good example that Srebrenica was totally demilitarised. It goes to his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I could understand that your question is attacking the witness's credibility in this aspect. But I still could not understand your questions about the 28th divisions. I don't think it's relevant to this case. It's not justified to any killings and deportations of Muslims from Srebrenica area. You may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, during the -- at one point, I believe it was on the 11th after you had left for Potocari, you were requested over the megaphone to report to the UN forces that were there, the DutchBat. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not demand anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your name was called to report.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you responded. You went there.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know what the whole thing was about really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to get to that. I was just about to say, you didn't know what was going to happen, but you showed up, and that's when you found out that they wanted you to be some sort of a representative for the folks that were -- had gathered over there.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you were somewhat concerned --

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent. Several times I sweated blood, I'd go to the toilet to wash my face. I'd go outside for some fresh air and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And of course, one of the reasons that you were apprehensive was because you didn't think that -- you didn't feel that you had the capacity to represent anyone or to speak for anyone for that matter?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several reasons. The way I remember it, Colonel Karremans, the commander of the Dutch battalion said roughly the following: "The Serb army wants official representatives of the local authorities in Srebrenica." I'm telling you what Colonel Karremans said. "We know that at this moment, these men can't be reached because they're already on their way through the woods." And then he kept silent. "The only thing we can do is to find someone in this group of refugees, and you were the obvious choice." I told him then that I was no official representative, that the whole thing was new to me, and that I was afraid myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But eventually you decided that you would go ahead, go to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Having been convinced by the commander of the Dutch battalion. He said he will help with our requests regarding the safe evacuation of all the people, the whole population. Those were the conditions that I agreed to, to go to the meeting in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You must have anticipated my follow-up question. That's what it was about. In fact, a precondition for you to attend that meeting was that you wanted them, meaning the DutchBat, to assist you in convincing General Mladic or whoever you would be meeting in the evacuation of the folks out of that area to the free territory. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Colonel Karremans also told General Mladic on that might about the overall situation in Potocari, the situation regarding the Bosniak refugees and the Dutch soldiers themselves. He talked about the need to provide food for the population in Potocari and also about the need to safely evacuate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I want to concentrate on what you told Karremans, Colonel Karremans, as a precondition to you attending the meeting. Your precondition was that you would attend provided they would assist you in promoting your agenda, which was the safe evacuation of those people out of that area to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This wasn't just my idea. There was a general need to do these things. It was a matter of survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the need of everyone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, but we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, I was in no position to dictate my terms to the Dutch battalion or the Serb army. I'm not sure what the essence of your question is really supposed to be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The essence is I'm trying to just get the truth. I just want to make sure that I understand that I'm speaking it correctly. And that is when you went to meet the DutchBat and they told you what they wanted you to do, you said that you would attend; however, you expected them to assist you in promoting what you believed needed to be done which was the evacuation, not the deportation, but the evacuation of those people because as you've just told us, that's what everybody thought was needed to be done because of the humanitarian crisis that was -- that was taking place in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to the interchanging of the terms evacuation and deportation and calling for a legal conclusion from this witness. That will take us down a road I don't think is appropriate or relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may respond quickly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday the gentleman did not miss an opportunity to characterise everything as a deportation. We have his statements; we have his testimony here today. And over and over he talks about evacuation. He wanted assistance to evacuate. So I'm trying to establish that. And there's a line of questioning that goes with it because if I get some leeway, perhaps I can tie it up for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I remember that during the testimony yesterday, the witness said both "evacuation" and "deportation." You may use both terms. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now yesterday, we saw a little clip of the video of the meeting that you held -- that you attended. And let me correct myself there, that you attended with Colonel Karremans when you met with General Mladic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you happen to see the entire video on Sunday when you met with Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it has been a while since you've seen it --

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the same thing I saw yesterday during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But what I'm saying is you've seen the entire video at one point.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Prior to that, in July 1995 obviously I was there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. I understand that. But we have a video of that meeting as well. And there was a question posed yesterday as to whether everything that was said during that meeting was captured on the video. So that's why I'm asking the question, if you're curious.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've ever seen the whole tape, and I'm not sure how much there was on it of the meeting itself. But certainly there must be details that were left outside of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it's -- as I understand it, it's your belief and understanding that during that meeting, you indicated to General Mladic that you wanted the safe evacuation of all the people under UNPROFOR supervision.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what Colonel Karremans said. To the best of my recollection, what I told General Mladic was about the numbers of refugees in the area, the numbers nearing 30.000, that they were mostly disabled people, elderly people, and so on. And I asked General Mladic, after Colonel Karremans had already spoken about the needs of those people, I asked him about the Serb army expelling the refugees from their homes, and I asked whether he believed, too, that evacuation was necessary to save the people's lives. In this critical situation, I told him that he must deal at the highest level with UNPROFOR and the International Red Cross. At that point, General Mladic interrupted me and said: "Please, write down, I want a handover of weapons by tomorrow morning" although he knew that I had nothing to do with weapons. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Have you had a chance to look at your statements before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly. I did not go through them very thoroughly if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what I mean. Just let me make sure I understand how many statements you gave. From reading one of your statements, it seems to indicate that you first gave a statement in Zagreb at the embassy. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By the way, do you have a copy of that statement?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a copy of that statement?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. But the statement itself is very similar to the one that I -- yes, but there's nothing new in that other statement. The gist is the same as in the other one, maybe the phrasing may have been a little different. My state in Zagreb, the condition that I was in in Bosnia in July 1995, we were shattered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you don't know whether the Prosecutor has that statement by any chance.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I am not exactly talking about this to the Prosecutor or to the Chamber for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just asked the question. Okay. Then you gave a statement in August -- I believe it was August 9, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember early August 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was to the State Security Service of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? That was in Tuzla. Right?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then as I understand it, there were a couple of other statements, but there was one five-page witness statement that you gave to a member of the Office of the Prosecution, and that was on September 5, 1995.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. That's possible. I can't remember the exact date, but that sounds plausible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I couldn't help notice that in some of these statements you're referring to Chetniks, Chetnik this, Chetnik that, everybody seems to be a Chetnik. And it seems to be when you're referring to Serbs. Can you explain to me what a Chetnik is.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact, I said we were shattered at that time. There was a collective tragedy that had taken place. There was a lot of sorrow. I may have been using the term Chetnik, but on the other hand during the war or after the war, you can hear such expressions used as a Turk or a balija. I'm really sorry for using that term but a lot of these terms are still in circulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or Ustasha for the Croatians.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I must say that I'm deeply sorry that there are people in Bosnia using such derogatory expressions at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But you don't -- as you said, that just because you're using that term doesn't mean that you have some universal hatred against all Serbs but it was something that was used during the war because of circumstances and what have you?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, quite the contrary. Even today, just like earlier, despite the tragedy of my town and my people, I still have friends, people with whom I'm on friendly terms. It's now down to us to build peace. I'm one of those people who remained in Bosnia under very different circumstances in order to build peace, but I need the assistance of others, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I guess what I'm trying to get at because this was an issue during the Krstic case, the use of the term Turk, the Court seemed to give that some sort of significance. And I take it by you using the word Chetnik doesn't necessarily mean a particular hatred that you hold against Serbs. It was just a term that was used during the war quite often to refer to the other side?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no hatred involved. I've seen many times in films the opposing sides using derogatory terms to refer to each other. Quite the contrary in my case, there was never any hatred in me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Getting back to the meeting, the first meeting that you attended, is it your recollection today that you never asked or suggested to General Mladic that the people should be evacuated and that it was just Karremans that made the suggestion?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karremans was the one who put forward the proposal. The next day when we arrived with the full Bosnian delegation at the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac, introductions were made. The new representatives were introduced. This took quite a while. And then General Mladic really ran the meeting and set the agenda. There was pressure being applied on us, the members of the Bosniak delegation in Bratunac. If memory serves me well, it was about 11.00 that someone from security or a soldier approached our table and said: "General, the Bosniaks have reached Bratunac on their own initiative what are we supposed to do?" And he said: "Send them to the stadium." You can understand what this meant for us under those conditions. May I remind you that in early April and May 1992, the Serb forces carried out executions of hundreds and hundreds of innocent civilians in Bratunac. They seized people, took them out of their homes and killed them. They were banking on the mental breakdown of the Bosniak people. They thought that we would start asking for mercy instead of resisting, and they wanted nothing to hamper them in their plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it that you were worried that there may be some retribution also for what perhaps you and Naser Oric were involved in on the orthodox Christmas in 1993 when you burned down a Serb village with Serbs in their homes being burned alive. So that might have been on your mind as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It's uncalled for him to accuse Nesib Mandzic of taking part in the Serb Kravica Christmas incident at this point. Personal attacks of this nature are absolutely uncalled for and I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with you. Mr. Karnavas, drop this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, but the indictment does indicate that his battalion -- his unit was involved --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry for interrupting him, but this kind of gratuitous comments designed to inflame the witness regarding this history is just uncalled for, and we have a long trial to go, and I hope it ceases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, just drop this question. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave on August 9th, 1993, it states here that you told the aggressor, General Mladic, that it would be best in this situation to evacuate the population safely to the free territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in vehicles and with an UNPROFOR escort. And to that General Mladic said: "Okay, I accept that. It's up to the people." And then it goes on. Now, do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. However, if Mr. Karnavas intends to impeach the witness, I think it would only be fair if he could direct the witness to the statement in B/C/S to allow the witness to look at what he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Do you have that transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have it here, Your Honour. Might I add, there are many different ways of impeaching. I was merely trying to refresh his memory at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you want to refresh his memory, please furnish that portion to the witness so the witness has a chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: However the Court wishes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a long statement. If you, perhaps with your interpreter, could help direct him to the spot, it might save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, no matter how you're trying to impeach me, I feel that I am an honourable man. I have never harmed anyone. Now, regarding the case before us, what I expected is to be asked questions about the deportations, about the massacre that took place in and around Srebrenica. I will answer your question, but really you have been trying to impeach me and destroy my credibility for quite some time now and show the Court, show me up as a man who is likely to adopt other people's opinions and quote other people. A gullible person. What I have been telling you, these were my words. This has taken us nowhere. We can talk on like this for days but still you wouldn't have the full picture of how the Bosniaks of Srebrenica suffered. So please go ahead and point me to the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you through, Mr. Mandzic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You should find it on page 11. Why don't you look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have the page in the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The page in the English version is page 9. It begins with: "I told the aggressor, General Mladic..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which line please roughly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It should be around line 20.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the lower half of the page, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, perhaps Ms. Tomanovic could point Mr. Mandzic in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There's another statement, the meeting -- that's toward the end of this meeting. Mr. Ibro Nuhanovic who was a member of the delegation on his way out pleaded with General Mladic on his way out. He said: "General, please let the people go. Look at these people. These here are all innocent people. They're hungry, tired, thirsty."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man I'm talking about did not survive the massacre in Srebrenica. He was not seen after the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, I'm merely trying to get you to acknowledge what you said in your statement. That's all. Now, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are -- there's more than what I remember as being written down here. There are further details what I've just said about Mr. Nuhanovic addressing General Mladic on his way out. The Dutch officers were already getting into the car. And he was pleading with General Mladic to let the people go. And General Mladic said nothing. I don't think this was recorded. You won't see this in the footage. This was on the way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right now, Mr. Mandzic, I'm referring to your statement, a statement that you gave. I suspect that you had an opportunity to read it and sign it to make sure that it was accurate. And as you've indicated before coming here today, you had an opportunity to read it, perhaps not carefully. Now, later on that page, later on, or it might be on the next page, you say, talking about the Chetnik General Mladic, where you say that "He indicated this time, I'm going to be merciful to everyone, release them, and help them go wherever they want." And then you say: "When I insisted that UNPROFOR should take on all responsibility for food, supplies, security, and evacuation, the Chetnik General broke off the meeting." That's what you put in your statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it after this meeting is when you had an opportunity to speak with a minister, Muratovic. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But he was in Tuzla, was he not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether he was in Tuzla, but they pointed me in his direction and said that he was on his way to Tuzla to attend a meeting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any direct connection. I did not have any approach to communications. I wanted to tell the international public and nationwide about what was going on in Srebrenica. We were completely cut off. We didn't even know whether anyone else outside the area knew about it. We weren't even sure that the Dutch battalion command were informing people or the international public about what was going on in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so I take it the Dutch battalion was not informing you what they were up to?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not us or others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not about the orders that they received, the orders that they received from their command or from the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or the reports that they were writing to the UN?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. Now, getting back to the minister, if it's okay with you --

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- this gentleman was with the government, was he not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, and you spoke to him asking him for some advice because after all, for better or for worse, you were more or less a negotiator?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a negotiator but not by choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But not by choice. But there you were. You're promoting to General Mladic for evacuation, and the minister gave you different instructions, did he not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And his instructions were that the refugees should stay where they are.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The wounded and the sick would be helicoptered out?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And according to my recollection, the government representative that you cite said: "Please be patient for another two hours. In another two hours, we're expecting an action by the French and English forces in order to protect the population." Unfortunately, you yourself know what the consequences were of those events. And I'm thinking about the activities of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't know what this conversation has to do anything with Mr. Muratovic or the killings in Srebrenica. Mr. Muratovic also wanted to help the Bosniaks, the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, by alarming the international community, the international institutions. But I allow for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you for allowing me to ask the question. And thank you for answering the question. And if we can go on to the next question, if that's okay with you, and --

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is allowed for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, now, later on, you indicate that you tried to stop the evacuation at that point, now that you had some sort of order from higher ups. But it was more or less too late because the evacuation had already commenced.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague Ibro Nuhanovic also attended these talks, and he also addressed Muratovic and said the situation was really dramatic. Serb officers and Serb soldiers were already deporting the people, beginning to separate the male population from the others and so on. The objective was to convey the situation in Srebrenica as dramatic and to ask for assistance from anybody in the world who would be in a position to offer any assistance to prevent the disappearance of a people from an enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I couldn't help but notice that this time you used the word "deportation." And if we look at your statement, you don't say that you went to the assistant commander of the Dutch battalion to stop the further deportation; you say to stop the further evacuation. Now, I take it when you wrote the statement out, you had an opportunity to choose your words very carefully. This is a very detailed, very articulate statement that you've made from a very educated individual. Do I take it in your mind at that time what was going on was an evacuation, and then you had your orders from the minister to stop the evacuation, to keep everybody there, and then you tried -- but it was too late to do anything about it because it had already commenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, the question is confusing, vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think before we rule that the witness used the word "evacuation" and "deportation" simultaneously almost yesterday during his testimony which means that the witness does not clearly distinguish the differences between the two words in his mind, not like you, not like me. So I hope you do not further confuse the witness on those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, yes, you are using the terms "evacuation" and "deportation" with the intention of proving to the Court that it was a voluntary evacuation here. Using the words "evacuation" or "deportation," we actually need to look the results or the consequences of these evacuations or deportations. This was a tragic deportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, I'm merely pointing out what you've stated in your statement. I'm using your words, the way you've characterised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I would hope counsel -- that's not a question, that's a statement. Could we have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's not spend much time on that wording. Please move on, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, there was a humanitarian crisis at the time, was there not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was one for years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I'm talking about that time. Work with me and we can get out of here as quickly as possible. On that particular day, or days, the 11th and 12th, there was a shortage of food, was there not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was a shortage of water, was there not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there hadn't been water for years, not only just that day. We were short of water for years. But still, we managed to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not talking about what happened in those years when you were in Srebrenica or the villages. I'm talking about on the 11th and the 12th when you're in Potocari and you have 25, 35, 40.000, whatever the number is of all those people gathered there. Do you agree with me that for those couple of days, the situation was very acute?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was dramatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one of the issues was how you're going to feed and how you're going to get water to all of these people.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had that same problem for years. But still, we managed to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic --

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in more difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you, Mr. Mandzic, you're an educated man. You're getting your Ph.D. or your masters. Certainly you can answer the question. I will repeat it. And if you don't understand the question, please let me know and I'll rephrase it. During those two days, there was a shortage of food in particular, was there not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During those two days, each of the refugees had with them food necessary for the next few days. This was the case with those who had gone through the woods and those who had gone to Potocari both. They had special supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So there was no humanitarian crisis as far as you're concerned with respect to food and water. Is that what you're saying here today?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas, but I think that you are twisting things around. Please don't do that. There had been a crisis for years. There was food for a few days. We were expecting humanitarian aid convoys, and these convoys were supposed to come to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. I understand that there was a crisis throughout the years, just as I understand that there was a black marketeering going on by your own admissions where forces were stealing foods, humanitarian food, selling it or keeping it for themselves and not passing it on to the people of Srebrenica. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, things like that happened also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One of your concerns during those days when you were negotiating with General Mladic was also to make sure that all the people there, all the refugees, had sufficient food and water. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The safety of the people was the first objective, their security of the population. But as far as food and the requirements for food for the Dutch soldiers, this was something that Colonel Karremans talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, were you aware -- I'll withdraw the question. The meeting itself, the first meeting that you attended, is it your testimony today that that was initiated by the DutchBat, or is it that you don't know who initiated the first meeting? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who it was. I couldn't confirm that. I know only that a Dutch officer or Colonel Karremans was the one who suggested that I be present. But I don't know who organised the meeting or who initiated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's time for a break. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, any cross-examination by Ms. Sinatra? Or yes, you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend and colleagues from the Prosecution, my name is Miodrag Stojanovic. We have an agreement for me to cross-examine today's witness. I will try in my first set of questions to go through a number of issues with the witness that the witness talked about in his testimony yesterday. The second set of questions will contain issues where I would like to have a yes or no answer from the witness for the sake of brevity. We hope to keep our cross-examination down and keep it shorter than Mr. Karnavas's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, yesterday in your testimony--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to yes or no answers. That would be very nice. But as long as the witness understands that he is clear to explain a yes or no answer, I think that is the more appropriate way to deal with it. They shouldn't be confined to yes or no. That's actually very difficult to ask a witness to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think we all understand that. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, you stated yesterday the night between the 10th and the 11th of July, we were at the school. We talked about what we should do. One group of people said that we should head for the woods, and there was another group who said we should head for Potocari. In view of what you said yesterday, and without doubting the authenticity of your statement, we wanted to ask you the following: Was there any preannounced plan, or preagreed plan, as to where people should go and who was the plan thought up by and who told you about the plan?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the second half of my testimony yesterday I said that there was no one who could tell anyone else to go through the woods or to Potocari, which means there was no such thing as a plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have to remind you that both you and the witness are speaking the same language. And whatever you said will be translated into English and French. So please pause after each question before you answer the question, Witness, and please wait for the interpretation until you start the next question. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. This applies equally to myself and to Mr. Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, does that mean that there was no plan for the men to head for the woods and women, children, elderly and disabled people, on the other hand, to head for the UN base in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such agreement until the 11th of July, we hoped that we would stay in the enclave and that the war would end finding us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How, then, do you explain the fact that the great majority of male refugees headed for Jaglic and Susnjari and most of the women, children, elderly and disabled people headed for the UN base?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those disabled, those who couldn't walk, they were the ones who headed for the UN base in order to get protection from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What about the men?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what their choice was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the men headed for Jaglic and Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were men aged between 15 and 70 who were also in Potocari. Thousands of such men. This was a matter of individual choice, and this applied to me, too. I got underway, too. I had undergone surgery a month before the fall of Srebrenica, and I was really tired and I could hardly walk but it was my choice to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a third possibility?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To go straight to heaven --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please pause for the sake of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which third choice you're referring to. Do you mean a third choice as in staying back in our homes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Or going to a third place?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third possibility would have been to stay in our homes but those houses were being torched and people were being killed in them. That would hardly have been a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday in response to a question by the Prosecutor, the enclave was mostly demilitarised. There was a presence of symbolic units carrying trophy weapons. In the same context, I wanted to ask you the following question, Mr. Mandzic: Are you aware of the fact that not even two months before the tragic events in Srebrenica, additional ammunition, weapons, and equipment were supplied to the members of the 28th division of the BH army stationed in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that a helicopter crashed and that some paramedics were killed in the crash. I'm not sure if it was in May or in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That helicopter, did it have anything to do with the supplies of military equipment or weapons?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can neither confirm nor deny this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I would try to show the witness the statement by Major Franken which he gave to the parliament commission at the Dutch parliament referring to this issue. And my next question will follow from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So at the meeting that was held before a commission of the Dutch parliament, Major Franken whom you also referred to yesterday, was asked the following question by a member of the parliamentary commission: "Was it possible that the 28th division took weapons that had been handed over during the demilitarisation?" And Major Franken replied, that was not only considered, this possibility, but the 28th division was even informed. Had they wish to do so, they could have come and collected everything from the collection point right there. However, they were not interested in that option. Furthermore, Major Franken goes on to say the following: "It is true that the weapons at the collection point were old and could hardly be used. They - meaning the 28th division - had much better and more up-to-date weapons." And he goes on to say, "I first became familiar with this piece of information when I saw the soldiers wearing brand-new uniforms. They were walking around in their brand-new combat uniforms carrying the latest model of Kalashnikovs. All of this took place in May, and soon after, the mysterious landing of a large plane at the Tuzla airport, very strange." That's what Major Franken said, and we shall have occasion to cross-examine him on that, I hope. My question to you now is: Having seen these facts, do you still abide by your statement yesterday that there were no units there, that the presence of units was symbolic and that they merely had trophy weapons as you phrased it?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you're asking this question as if I was a general in the army or the commander of the division at the time. To the best of my recollection, in Srebrenica in early April or early May 1993, there had been a demilitarisation, the result of which --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. My apologies. We maybe straying further and further away from the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be allowed to answer the question unless he's getting into some extremely prejudicial area, but he was just answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, you have to wait for the witness to answer the question. We are interested in his answer. Witness, you may continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Furthermore, I was not even a member of the staff that you're referring to at that time. I was not even a member of those units as a soldier. I was the principal of the local secondary school. My job was the education of children under those difficult circumstances. And I must emphasise, there were people that was not exactly on friendly terms with, such people as Naser Oric first and foremost. Now all these issues relate to supplies of weapons, there's no connection between me and that. I do know, however, that there were units that the enclave had been defended and that 10.000 people got killed. So as I said, the demilitarisation was carried out. For the most part, artillery, anti-aircraft, anti-tank weapons had been handed over. If there was such a heavy presence of those units that you're referring to, I don't think 10.000 people would have been killed. Now, as to what Major Franken said about that, I don't think that applies to me necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want us to have equal rights in this respect, and I fully accept everything that the witness has just stated. My conclusion is that he's not competent to judge whether the area had indeed been demilitarised or not. He did not hold a position of military authority that would have enabled him to draw any conclusions in that respect. What he said yesterday is what I have just quoted. He said the area was demilitarised and the only weapons present in the area were trophy weapons, whereas today we have the witness stating that he does not really know this. Secondly, these were not my words. I was quoting Major Franken. I'm not sure what the situation was there at that time. I have no further questions regarding this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think there's some misunderstandings between the counsel and the witness. This witness will tell us what he saw, what he did, what he felt at that time. And we, the Judges, will make a judgement on whether it's true or not. We understand that there's some discrepancy between your question and the witness's answer, but that is normal in those proceedings. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just another question regarding your testimony yesterday,

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDZIC
utterances.text: At one point, you said inside the base, there was a line which restricted movement inside the base and which directed civilians on their way to the buses. Can you please just tell us who set those lines and who was it that restricted the movement of civilians inside the base?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure who put those lines down, but certainly the movement of refugees was restricted to that particular corridor towards the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May I therefore conclude that you have no idea who put those lines down?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I have no idea. I didn't say that I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In today's testimony, you answered Mr. Karnavas's questions regarding the statement that you gave to the state security sector in Tuzla on the 9th of August. Can I conclude that you accept the statement as authentic and that you have recognised your signature on the statement?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I take it for a fact that this took place on the 9th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed you could say that. I can't remember the exact date, but it was in early August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I take it for a fact that your recollection of those tragic events was then clearer perhaps than it is today?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but also more vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain the Court what you mean by saying "more vulnerable"?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Please try to understand what vulnerability means. In those tragic days of July 1995, each of the survivors, all the mothers awaiting the return of their sons, all the wives awaiting their brothers were totally lost, an expectation and fear of their destiny. It was difficult to get their bearings in their new environment. On the other hand, despite this vulnerability, we were hopeful that most of the people who had been held at the camp in Potocari or those who had crossed the woods --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Without meaning to interrupt the witness, Your Honours, what I wanted to say is my understanding of the term vulnerability, you were referring to your own statement?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That has nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Questions and answers are overlapping. We cannot get what you are saying. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He asked the witness what he meant by vulnerability. This is a broad and open-ended question which the witness was attempting to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just explain, when is a person vulnerable, after they have lost somebody or five years later?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The question was whether this meant that in some ways because of this vulnerability you are not standing by your statement from August 1995?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So can I just say rather than repeating the question, part of the question that Mr. Karnavas had already asked, is it correct that on the 25th of July, together with 500 soldiers, 500 guns, and about one million bullets, you arrived from the free territory of Tuzla in Srebrenica in order to organise a resistance together with Nurif Rizvanovic, and that you were carrying out the duties of the assistant to the commanding officer of the battalion and that you were wounded in 1993 near Skelani on Mount Malteski Vis?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what operation was it in Skelani or near Skelani in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, that was an operation of the BH army units in Srebrenica for their houses. Of course, there were certain civilians that were killed in these operations, and I'm very sorry about. That's not something that we can deny.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that my conclusion is correct, that was an attack on Skelani with the purpose of getting hold of Skelani and returning people to their houses? Am I correct in saying that there were people killed on both sides?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just explain. Skelani is more than 75 per cent Bosniak, according to the census from 1991. And you can correctly understand that the wish of these people was to return to their homes, to their area. They were exiled, they had no food, there were no medicines, it was very hard for them to live in other people's houses. And naturally in that operation, as I've already explained, there were clashes, there were people who were wounded on both sides, there were victims on both sides, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I to understand that that was an attack on the place called Skelani, this operation that you were wounded in?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no I was wounded much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So it's a different operation?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was wounded much later. I was wounded on the 25th of January during the attack of the JNA. There was a Novi Sad unit attacking this elevation that you've just described during the shelling in the Tar area by the Yugoslav army troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please, stop here. I think you made a very difficult time for the interpreters. There's no hurry. And I believe that the counsel should be more mindful of the pause so to keep the pace of questioning and answering. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We're going to try and coordinate better the question and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned today that in Skelani, there were 75 per cent of Bosniak population. Is it correct the last official census that was carried out in Bosnia-Herzegovina was in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the results of the population census carried out in the municipality of Srebrenica in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was the structure of the population in the municipality of Srebrenica according to the census in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 75 per cent Bosniaks, 23 per cent Serbs, and then 2 or 3 per cent the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These are official statistics that were obtained by the then Yugoslav statistics institute. In June and July of 1995, can you tell me whether in the demilitarised area of Srebrenica there was a percentage of 23 per cent Serbs present?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were perhaps several dozens. I'm not quite sure. In the beginning of the demilitarisation, there were several dozens of citizens of Serb nationality, Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Several dozens of Serbs in the entire Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A demilitarised area?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who found themselves in a very difficult situation with their neighbours who were Bosniaks from the beginning of the war until the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the rest, 20, 22 per cent of Serbs according to the census from 1991?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning of April of 1992, in the neighbouring municipality of Bratunac, there were thousands of paramilitary units that arrived from Yugoslavia. There were units of Yugoslav army corps that arrived and similar thing happened in the municipality of Srebrenica, also in the municipality of Bajna Basta which is in the territory of Yugoslavia, thousands of military -- paramilitary formations arriving from Yugoslavia. Beginning of April 1992, the Serb Territorial Defence carried out offensive operations towards the town area and the neighbouring villages forcing thousands of Bosniaks from Srebrenica town area to leave it. So they left the area, and most of them went to Tuzla and abroad, starting from April 1992. Even to date, they're either in Tuzla, Sarajevo, or abroad. After some three weeks, units of the Territorial Defence of the Srebrenica municipality, mostly made up of Bosniaks, organised themselves, started resisting, and this is when the first clashes started, the first shootings on the edges of the town. And Serb units that were in Srebrenica in April 1992 in such a short period of time during those three weeks killed about 80 civilians, 80 old men. Frightened by the reaction of the Bosniak side, they took the entire population with them from that area, apart from several dozens who stayed, as I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
