utterances.text: Am I to understand that it is correct that this percentage of 22 per cent approximately citizens of Serb nationality, because of the war operations and because of their personal lack of security, they left?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot speak about the 22, because that's the entire municipality. We're speaking about the demilitarised zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the demilitarised zone.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we're speaking about 10 per cent, not 22 but 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And they left that area because of these reasons?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mostly forced by these units, whether they were military, paramilitary units, they were forced to leave the town. But before that there were exchanges of fire, at least according to what the other people said because at the time I was not in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Within that context, could you tell the Trial Chamber what happened during that time to some of the members of the Zec family in 1993 in the demilitarised area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I remember that incident. We say "incident" but in fact it's a tragedy for the Zec family. There was a soldier or something else, or he was just a maniac. He killed mother and a son from the Zec family. And at the time, I was wounded in that time. I was in rehabilitation, and I heard about it. And I'm not just saying this, that I was humane, but thousands of people were condemning this murderer. And I think that this murderer was later arrested. He was taken to trial in Tuzla. But on the other hand, the murder of the members of the Zec family is a tragedy for the Zec family. But such individual murders cannot be compared to a mass liquidation, execution of Bosniaks and the tragedy of Bosniaks. But I am saying this with full sincerity here before this Trial Chamber, I'm speaking as a man who feels great solidarity with these people, after the war I was able to meet some members of Zec family. I expressed my condolences and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not here making a -- I'm not justifying a crime with a crime. I'm not saying that. I think we are both trying here to come to what the truth is. I will come back to the statement that we started from, Your Honour. Am I to understand that it is true that in the summer of 1993, at the initiative of Hamdo Efendic and Mustafic Ibran, from the institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former chief of the public security station, you put together an initiative committee and that you started activating the party that had been banned and that you were personally involved?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but then we were dispersed, we were told to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But bearing in mind that you're an intellectual, that you're a lecturer, that you're a teacher, a soldier, that you were also -- had also been wounded and a political activist and we agreed that you had been all these things, should I conclude that this was the reason why members of the Dutch battalion set you aside, took you out of that mass of people in Potocari and said, "This person could represent the Bosniaks, although he is not an authority"?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot make that conclusion in reference to myself. But I know that on that day, 11th of July, the Dutch officer Major Boering saw me. And whether he recalled seeing my name or my face, and then he introduced me to the colonel and the colonel accepted that, I don't know. I'm not going into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking this because yesterday, the witness said that he thought that that's how he became involved, that Major Boering - I'm sorry about the pronunciation for the interpreters - because he had known him from the school and he had known him as a man and that's why this was the reaction. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have to interrupt, that is just too fast. We have to bear in mind that this is the International Tribunal. Maybe it is a disadvantage of this Tribunal that everything you says has to be translated into another two languages. Witness, I understand that you're eager to give your evidence, and I have promised you that we will send you home today. But just wait until we have translation of the question. Then you answer that question. Just wait for a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. Yes, of course, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I will try and finish very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a question in relation to this statement. You said on page 14, last paragraph. May I?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That you're concluding that UNPROFOR had helped the aggressor in the intention of cleansing the enclave from the Bosniak population just for the purpose of getting their soldiers out of Srebrenica. This conclusion of yours, does it still stand today?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the last paragraph? Can you please read the entire sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll go slowly. So the sentence is: "The conclusion is that the UNPROFOR, among other things, helped - and I'm quoting - helped the aggressor in their intention to cleanse the enclave from the Bosniak population just so that their soldiers could be gotten out of Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you direct us to the English portion of that by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honours. This is on page 11 of the English version. May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Which line, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last paragraph, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So my question was do you still stand by that conclusion today?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, and everyone else, allow me to read this in my own mother tongue, this last paragraph. "All the facts stated above as well as the previous actions of the UNPROFOR command in the Srebrenica enclave point to the conclusion that the Chetniks had informed UNPROFOR that the Srebrenica enclave would be attacked. They left or donated to the Chetniks about 30 transport and combat vehicles, hundreds of pieces of infantry weapons, other equipment, food, and so on. And that they assisted the aggressor in their intention to cleanse the enclave of Bosniaks just so they could pull out their soldiers out of Srebrenica." This paragraph, I will explain it. According to the UNPROFOR mandate previously established, it was their mission to prevent, that is to ensure the safety of the population inside the enclave, as well as to supply the population with food and any other needs they had. When the attack of the VRS occurred, beginning of July or the end of June, as far as I was able to hear, they left the weapons, equipment at the place of the attack. Further on, when there were more aggressive attacks of the VRS, this caused the mass exodus of population from their homesteads. They did not establish checkpoints. And I'm not saying that they should have engaged VRS in combat, but it is true that they were supposed to stop, or rather along those directions, those roads where the transports of the VRS were going, they were supposed to prevent them from moving into the town. Further on, on the 21st of July when they crossed, and I mean the crossing of the soldiers and the equipment of the DutchBat, across the border into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I saw that personally as the vehicle -- convoy was going to the other side, and I felt it was a gift of that army to the army of Yugoslavia for cooperation. I don't know what cooperation it was, but it was catastrophic. Furthermore, the equipment that was left behind in other locations, equipment left by Dutch soldiers, will enable the VRS to use this technical equipment, to use combat equipment, with UN insignia and call on to Bosniaks to come out and surrender, making them believe that they were UN forces. And later on execute them. From all this, we can conclude that they did not resist the separation of the male population in Potocari. They partly assisted the Serb army while they were cleansing the enclave. And I'll still stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Along the same lines, just one further question: You said, yesterday as well as today, that part of the patrolling station units of the Dutch battalion had surrendered to the Chetniks or withdrew towards the town itself. Do you know this for a fact, that they, in fact, surrendered or do you just assume that they surrendered? The Dutch in their statement claim that they were, in fact, captured.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now as to whether they surrendered or were captured, I'm not familiar with the details. But I also know that on the 12th of July -- oh, yes, right. Excuse me. May I continue now, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure if they surrendered or were, in fact, captured. But I do know that the commander of the Dutch battalion on the 11th of July in the evening, when he called me to explain the situation, he said that they were facing difficulty, too, that they had some of their own who had been captured in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nesib, am I to conclude that you are not certain whether those soldiers surrendered or were, in fact, captured?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see for myself therefore I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just comparing this to your actual statement. Thank you. Just one further question, I'm about to bring my cross-examination to an end, we are here defending Lieutenant-Colonel Jokic. I wanted to ask you whether you personally know Dragan Jokic, whether you have ever seen the man?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can neither deny nor confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no further questions at this stage. We wish to thank the witness on behalf of Dragan Jokic's Defence. We hope that we have not hurt your feelings in any way because certainly that was not our intention. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, at the time when the tragic events in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica took place, have you been a member of the CDA.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to the party statute, I was a member of the SDA, a member of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Did you belong to the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could call it that, I suppose. I never really received a proper membership card. We had no other choice than to resist. Even while resisting and after we had put up resistance, several thousands of innocent people were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: On the 17th July, 1995, you signed a declaration, on the evacuation from the enclave, Srebrenica enclave. What was -- describe once more, what was the situation when this declaration was signed by yourself.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about the situation yesterday. I will try to describe it again. On the 12th, 13th, and 14th -- on the 11th, 12th, and 13th of July, there was a mass deportation taking place. Between the 13th and 17th, there were dozens of severely wounded people left, elderly people aged about 70, as well as those who were young aged, between 20 and 30. Between the 12th and the 21st of July, a group of about 26 Bosniaks remained in the base of the Dutch battalion with Serb soldiers and officers entering the base every single day aiming at creating psychological pressure, exerting pressure on the Bosniaks still there, on their families. Those few remaining families, their aim was to exert pressure on the wounded. On the other hand the MSF who were also present at the base, at that time, or rather their representatives, informed us that the Serb forces had taken some of the wounded off the convoy in Bratunac, that is, at the line of delineation between Bratunac and Kladanj. This was the situation in those critical days. The Bosniaks were threatened by General Mladic. He had threatened several days before that. He said that they would either stay or vanish, and indeed vanish is exactly what they did. In this situation, the Dutch soldiers were mainly looking for a way to get out of the enclave with no regard for all the people who had managed to cross to the BH army-controlled territory, or rather, the territory under the control of the Bosnian civilian authorities. We were left to our own devices, or rather, left in the lurch. Not one of us had any faith in survival. Right behind my back, I see a witness of those tragic events, a Bosniak man, who was also scared, I believe, and didn't know where to go or where to turn. In such moments, or rather on that critical day, the 17th of July, before the signing of this, I saw a number of Serb officers entering the building and staying, according to my estimate, perhaps one or two hours. Mr. Deronjic then arrived with this statement that they had drawn up. It was a request actually to evacuate the wounded and that group including 26 Bosniaks. What they could add to that document at that time was the last part of the sentence, yes, as concerns UNPROFOR escort. This escort was carried out on the first day, the 11th of July. And those first buses, between 14 and 1600 hours, and this escort, they were disarmed by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Mandzic, I would like to ask you whether you personally were threatened before and while signing this declaration.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They threatened before. As I said yesterday, there were soldiers coming and going and approaching the group with 26 Bosniaks. They asked me personally if I had taken part in this or that operation. I wasn't even in the area at that time. And they were investigating other Bosniaks, too. On the other hand, outside the base, several metres from away from the fence, there were Serb guards stationed there. They were watching us, exerting pressure by their presence. However, I must say that there were soldiers who were asking me questions about where I was and what I did, and one of told me if you had been at Zlaca, I would kill you on the spot. Perhaps he was a survivor of that particular operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: As far as I understand, you negotiated with militaries, with General Mladic and other militaries. And then explain me why this declaration was signed on the Serb part by Miroslav Deronjic, civil commissioner for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can hardly be expected to explain this. I don't know what the orders were. I don't know what influence Deronjic could exert at that time. I didn't know what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And for how long did you act as representative of the civilian authorities of the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never been a representative until July 1995. I've already said this. I was never in the government, the executive or the legislative government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Maybe my question was not clear enough. You signed this declaration as representative of the civilian authorities of the enclave of Srebrenica. And since that day, how long you acted as representative of civilian authorities of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for a single moment actually. I was never appointed by anyone. I was never authorised. The conditions were not there for us to act on behalf of the civilian authorities. Please, Your Honours, this statement, or rather the allegation stating that I was a civilian representative for the Bosniak side, the phrasing itself is invalid. And it was coercion of the members. We should ask ourselves the following question: "What about the other two members of the Bosniak delegation? What became of them?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Have you ever met the persons which you believe participated in committing the crimes in Srebrenica enclave before you signed this declaration or after?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met some people in the period when I held an executive office in Srebrenica, between 1999 and 2001. People responsible for crimes against civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Can you name those people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe we could have the last answer redacted. Now, Witness, I have a question for you. During your testimony yesterday and today, you mentioned Serb soldiers, Serb forces, and Serb guards. Do you happen to know which unit those Serb soldiers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: NESIB MANDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really can't say. I don't know. From what I could tell back then, they were all wearing the same uniforms and same insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions out of Judges' questions? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I do have a question, but it was a question that I should have asked. You know, I don't know if I'm permitted to ask the question. In other words, it's not a rebuttal to a question asked by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid not. I think if you want to ask some questions, you have to be strictly within the scope of the questions the Judge asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's why I didn't ask for that permission, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At this stage, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have a list here. It's various video stills and the three declarations and perhaps it's simpler just to provide this to the registry than read them all out unless there's an objection on a particular item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have got that list. I just want to make sure whether Defence team got that list or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We did receive the list, Your Honour. We have no objections to the Prosecution tendering the items from the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Your Honour, we would like to tender the document that we showed to the witness today, and that would be his statement from August 9th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me do the job one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I just ask Mr. Stojanovic, you know, whether you have any objections to the documents tendered by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. So the documents tendered by the Prosecution from P27 to P36.2/B have been admitted into evidence. Are there any objections concerning the document tendered by Mr. Karnavas, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think it's a hearsay document, and it's -- there's quite a bit more in that document that was not addressed. And if the Court accepts that document, I believe they should accept all the various statements, to put it in full context. And I don't know if this Trial Chamber would like all the statements of the various witnesses as I know the previous Trial Chamber wanted. That, I don't have a real objection to. But as picking and choosing documents, I would object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could respond. There's no picking and there's no choosing. I used the document because the gentleman obviously needed to have either his memory refreshed or to be confronted with it. Frankly, I have no objections to the Trial Chamber receiving all of the statements made by the gentleman, and I would also urge the Court to look at his entire testimony from the Krstic trial. There's lots of areas that weren't discovered -- discussed today in those statements. And also, if I may address Mr. McCloskey's comment with respect to the hearsay aspect and areas that weren't covered. First of all, the witness recognised the document, recognised it as one that he had read before he came here. And certainly if Mr. McCloskey thought that there was something in the document that he needed to have addressed, he could have addressed it. But by and large, it was this gentleman's statement, it was made contemporaneous to the events, slightly thereafter, and as I have indicated, I've absolutely no objection, there's no picking or choosing and I have no problem hereon to introduce every document that I can think of irrespective of whether it's necessary or not, if that's what the Prosecution wishes for me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think you have some reasons behind your statement just now. And we don't think it's hearsay evidence. But as a normal practice, Mr. Karnavas, I have to say that we have this witness live, testifying to us, about the incidents which happened there. And this statement has been extensively used and quoted during the cross-examination, and all the points are in the transcript now. So we don't think it's necessary to admit the previous statement into the evidence, except in a very extraordinary circumstances. So this document is not admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. We had the same thoughts about the statement that Mr. Karnavas talked about. But having in mind the witness's testimony today, we think that the Court's ruling is acceptable. Most of it has indeed been reflected in the transcript. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to interrupt, and I do apologise. In keeping with the Court's ruling, as I indicated, there was one question that I didn't ask that I should have asked, that I could not ask in rebuttal. Because in the statement at the final paragraph, the gentleman gives a description of his opinion as to the fall of Srebrenica where he talks specifically about the commander, his commander, Naser Oric, who wasn't there at the time and that there was a fear on the part of -- potential fear on the part of the Chetniks that Naser Oric may be coming from Tuzla to take over or to do -- to confront the troops over there, the Serb troops. So in light of that, Your Honour, I would request that the item be introduced into evidence, and if not, to at least take into consideration that in the last paragraph of the statement, this gentleman gives his opinion and he specifically refers to the Commander Naser Oric. So at that time, he knew that Naser Oric was a commander, a commander of the 28th division who at the time wasn't in Srebrenica but was of Srebrenica. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think this question should be raised during your cross-examination. We gave you the opportunities to do that, and we have already made a ruling that this previous statement will not be admitted into the evidence. But anyway, your remarks are in the transcript. Witness, thank you very much for coming here to give your evidence. I apologise once again for the inconvenience during the proceedings brought to you, and I wish you good luck in your future and a pleasant journey back home. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now, before we have the next witness, could we have a break at this moment so that everybody could prepare for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's your courtroom, Your Honour. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll resume at 40 minutes past 5.00, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before we hear this witness, Ms. Sinatra, do you have a matter to bring to the attention of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's only an administrative matter that deals with access of Defence counsel to the Defence room at breaks. I've brought it to the attention of the Registry once before, but after hours when we have a break, Defence counsel has no access to get to the Defence room once the cafeteria is closed and locked up, and our badges don't allow us to go through any of the areas that are prohibited from red badges. So we can't get down there without an escort and we can't get up because everything is locked again. I was wondering if the Court could please assist us in solving this problem before tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course, I will consult with the Registrar on this matter and ask them to see to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So Mr. Waespi, are you ready for the direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, or rather, good evening, Your Honours. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand Mr. President that his solemn declaration which he gave in closed session, of course, is binding because we are now in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There is no problem about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, can you please spell out your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Boering. Bravo, Oscar, Echo, Romeo, India, November, Golf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you are of Dutch nationality?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you were born on 6 May, 1959?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in terms of your career, military career, you attended the Dutch royal military academy in Breda from 1978 to 1982?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I understand that you're an artillery officer by specialisation?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also served after Srebrenica as a major in the Dutch Brigade in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: For how long was that detail?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Half a year in early 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you've done operations and planning at brigade level. Of course, you were a deputy G3 for three years?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And currently, you are stationed with the high readiness headquarters First German-Netherlands Corps in Muenster, Germany?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you are, as a staff officer, responsible for policy matters?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would just like to bring to the Court's attention that the Prosecution is asking completely leading questions during their direct examination of their witness. But if we could have an agreement that once they get through the introduction part of Mr. Boering's testimony that the leading questions would end and they go back to asking direct questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think those questions are only concerning the background of this witness. To save time, the Prosecution is allowed to ask the questions along this line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: We agree with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But as you rightly pointed out, when we come to substantive matters, the Prosecution will try to avoid any leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In fact, that was my last leading question, I hope. And we'll turn to Srebrenica 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, for how long were you in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Half a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you state the exact dates?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Early January until 13 June, 1995 -- excuse me, July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, since you're the first officer from the Dutch army testifying in this case, I think it would be useful if you could tell the Trial Chamber the role of DutchBat, briefly outline the structure, and for instance the number of troops. But perhaps we can start with the mandate of DutchBat as you saw it for that half a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Waespi, I think that question is too long. You have to break it one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I entirely agree with Your Honour. I asked Mr. Boering just to concentrate on the mandate of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the mandate is concerned, first of all we were there, to put it in English, to secure a safe area. Second, we were there to demilitarise the enclave. Third, we were there to provide humanitarian assistance if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us the number of companies or other troop units you had at that time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The closest staff company, two companies that were serving a mission in the enclave, the Bravo and the Charlie companies. One company was stationed in Potocari, and the other was stationed in Srebrenica. All together, approximately 450 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What type of weapons did DutchBat have at that time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Light infantry arms with APCs with limited armour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could just show us the locations of the companies and units you just outlined on Prosecution Exhibit P20.1. And hopefully, you can see it on your screen.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Not yet. In fact, one company in Potocari, primarily to protect the northern area, and one company in Srebrenica, primarily for the southern area. And the overview shows various letters, and that's where the actual physical observation posts were set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So by those letters, you mean the letters starting on top of the enclave with an N and an O.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, November and Oscar, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us the role of these observation points?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It was a small deployment of about eight men, and their task was to observe the area from that area and to conduct limited patrols and to report activities, both from outside and from inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Boering, in terms of the armed forces, the troops in that area, where were the forces stationed?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Which troops do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Which troops were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: When you're speaking about the BSA troops, there were in fact three degrees, located at Bratunac Brigade, a Milici Brigade, and here in the south, Zeleni Jadar. And they were part of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. How about the BH army?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The BH army, to the extent that we could refer to that as an army, we had light arms. I was primarily in contact with the supervisory structure that was present. And the area was divided into various subsections. But I was not in direct contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boering. Can you briefly talk about the degree of organisation and strength as you saw it of the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The organisation was, in fact, an organised Drina Corps with a clear rigid system of command. And what I saw of the Bratunac Brigade, it was a clear structure with sufficient staff and arms in the sense of artillery and tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you make some observations about the BH army.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: What I saw and heard indirectly about operations, it was lightly armed, primarily hand-fire arms, and machine-guns and limited other arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Major Boering, let's turn to your function. What was your role in 1995 in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The role was to serve as the liaison on behalf of the battalion staff, both toward the Serbs and the Muslims in the enclave. Toward both local authorities and military authorities. At that level, I dealt with both structures, both civil and military. In addition, within the enclave, I dealt with NGO organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What kind of NGO organisations did you have contacts with?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: UNHCR, MSF, the Red Cross, and a few others that don't come to mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall what MSF stands for?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Medicine Sans Frontier, doctors without borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, you said that you were meeting with military authorities. Now, did you have an initial meeting in January 1995 with the representatives from the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that was in Bratunac upon the transfer of DutchBat II to DutchBat III. All authorities were present there, the Drina Corps commander, General Zivanovic, and the various brigades that I mentioned earlier, the contacts with us for the Bratunac brigade, that was Major Nikolic. For Milici, it was Major Sakic. Let me think. For the Skelani unit, it was Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall what was discussed during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At the meeting, the role of DutchBat was discussed, especially with respect to demilitarisation. And General Zivanovic explained that we were clearly entitled to the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall what exactly he told you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Not exactly, but in the sense that he had lived in the neighbourhood of Srebrenica as a family member and was, therefore, entitled to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, let's talk now about the situation in the beginning of July 1995. Where were you personally stationed in that period?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I was stationed at the headquarters in Potocari in early July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, during that period, do you recall, observe, activity around the civilian houses near the compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. In early July, there was shelling from the Bratunac area with heavy machine-gun fire, sometimes with light mortar shells, on houses that we could see from our compound. That was in that area. And as for the southern area, what I'm indicating now, the southern area over here, in this area, there was also shelling in early July. And the population fled from there towards Srebrenica. And some of those observation posts came under attack as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boering. Just referring back to what you said about "these houses in Potocari," in your opinion at that time, were those military targets?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, those were, in fact, physically inhabited houses. Families lived in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, going to the second part of your answer, you said that you also were aware of movements of civilians towards Srebrenica from the south side. Now, can you explain to the Court why this happened.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: In some way, my interpretation is, I think, that it became impossible for the population to continue living there. And in that way, the population was forced to move towards Srebrenica. And there, they were made to feel unsafe as well so that they might be transported out of the enclave in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the factors were in your opinion why it was made impossible, to quote you, for the population to continue living there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Actual shelling by artillery, mortar shells, and houses that had been taken were set on fire. This was not my own perception; I heard this indirectly, that when people remained behind, they were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when you talk about artillery and mortar shells, from which army were these fired from?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Especially by the BSA toward Bratunac, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you talked about executions and that you only heard about it.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Somebody who was with our own battalion at the time, whether it was execution or firing in which the shooting was directed at a certain target. I'd go with the second, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, have you heard of a Serbian shelter project?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Swedish shelter project?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, I'm sorry. The Swedish shelter project.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. That's houses built in the south of this area, especially for the refugees. And that camp was the first to be attacked around the 8th of July, and the population moved from there towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were residing in that Swedish shelter project?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Not exactly, but certainly 5.000 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to go to Srebrenica yourself?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Several times. That was part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, at that time, when the refugees were pouring into Srebrenica, as you just outlined, were you in Srebrenica as well?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At the time I went to Srebrenica primarily because of the tension in the southern area, and that was, like I said before, combined with the company in Srebrenica. So I was operating from that command post in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what was your function there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If there were indeed problems with both -- either the Muslim authorities, especially the first group to coordinate matters, one example was a blocking position in Srebrenica, and the BiH soldiers were trying to block the vehicle by -- through threatening with anti-tank weapons. So there was no freedom of action, which we do need to act. At that point, I drove there to resolve the situation together with the Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you, Major Boering, could briefly refer to the map and explain where these blocking positions were established by DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Pointing out blocking positions is a bit difficult. But in fact, effectively along this route, various points were set out. You can see one in front of here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we cannot see when you're pointing to your screen. So please explain referring to the map where you're pointing to.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Okay. It's the route between the Swedish shelter project and Srebrenica where at the bottom you see several pink triangles, and moving up to the north, you see the city of Srebrenica, and there you see the black line, which is a road. And along that road, we took various blocking positions up to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is it fair to say in relation to the red dot with the letter "G" that these blocking positions were between spot G and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: They started more to the south, but they culminated in the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Waespi, I think the best way to show that exact point is to furnish a map to the witness, and let the witness mark on that map and put it on the ELMO, that is the traditional way. Otherwise, it's a little bit difficult, you know, for us to know the exact place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour. We tried this wonderful fancy project Sanction, but occasionally it does have some disadvantages. If you could move it a little bit up, I guess, so -- Srebrenica should be in the middle if you can manage that. Yes, that's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps, Major Boering, if you could start by telling us, indicating where the Swedish shelter project was.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Here at these triangles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could you maybe indicate it with a cross.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it's a small cross. I hope it's visible. And perhaps the letters "SSP."

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then the blocking positions.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [Marks] Along this road, there are positions facing south.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And of what type of armour or weapon or material did these blocking position consist of?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: APCs. And occasionally a Mercedes Benz.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How do you evaluate that from a military perspective?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: More to report than as an actual deterrent, as a deterrent through the armour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what are the dates now we are talking about when these blocking positions were established?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: From the 9th of July, as far as I can remember, because this Swedish shelter project was abandoned from the 8th. And around that date, Echo was attacked at the observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, at the end when these blocking positions got closer and closer to Srebrenica, as I understand you, were the observation points in the south still established?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No. Some of these posts had been abandoned or our personnel had been taken prisoner or hostage. Hostage rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's turn, Major Boering, to the events of July. The night before, did you have a meeting in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, the battalion staff, and also with Colonel Karremans present, and we had a meeting with the leadership of the enclave in Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: To discuss the situation. And actually, that evening, air support was more or less promised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Why was air support requested or promised, as you said?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It was promised if the attack were to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did air support actually happen?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Very late and to a very limited extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was the situation in Srebrenica at that time? How many people were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: 30.000, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what time, are you talking about what day now?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: We're now talking about the 10th and the 11th, so the population from the Swedish shelter project and the surrounding villages had all moved towards Srebrenica. They were staying there in the streets, uncertain as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was the atmosphere as you recall it?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The population was almost desperate. There was a lack of food and drink. And it was unclear what the future was going to be like. And around town, one could hear a lot of shooting of mortars and lighter armour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to briefly review a clip of a video which we have already seen. Just perhaps 20 seconds, if that could be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Boering --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- do you recall these scenes, Mr. Boering?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this. I was walking through that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there any shelling into the area of the UN Compound in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that actually happened. And I recall an injured person, a boy about 10 years old, who was brought into a medical care post. And he had mortar shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was that the only casualty that occurred at that time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No. There were more, but I cannot tell you a precise number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, before we leave the area, just going back to the meeting you talked about with your superior Colonel Karremans, who were the participants of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Present were Colonel Karremans, Officer Rave and myself. And from the Muslim population, a number of people from the civilian population, and some from the military planning group. And from the local population, there was Fahrudin, and from the military, as far as I remember, Ekrem was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was Ekrem?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At least he was the security officer. And in the absence of other commanders, he also was in command temporarily. And I don't remember precisely, but I believe that Ramic was also there, and he was the actual chief of staff of the BH army there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Major Boering, you talked about the shelling of the area around the compound in Srebrenica and the casualty of that little boy. Were these casualties just accidental casualties, or you as a specialised artillery officer, did you form an opinion at that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just object here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise for the objection, but I think there's a lack of foundation. The witness indicated that he did not witness the shelling that caused injury to the boy. Perhaps a foundation could be laid, the particular question could be posed. But at this moment I'm afraid there's a lack of foundation, and I'm not sure that the witness is competent to answer that question the way it's phrased in the manner in which it is phrased and without the foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think in answering the question put by the Prosecutor, the witness said that around the town, there was some shellings. And then the Prosecutor asked a further question, whether the shellings happened in the city, in Srebrenica itself. The witness answered that yes. I think this is the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please repeat the question for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. You are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Major Boering, you as an artillery specialist, you were present when shelling happened I understand?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you saw these casualties. Did you form an opinion at that time whether these casualties were accidental or done on purpose?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The opinion I had about this was that it was intentional, on purpose, as I said before, particularly aimed at giving the population the feeling that they were insecure. And thereby -- let me put it this way: Making them want to leave the enclave in order to become safe. To give you an example, on my own account, if I myself when I was moving around, I was also regularly shot at. But, say, well, they just missed in order to give me a feeling of like "don't do this again." And when after that I got in touch with the Serbian post, they actually indicated this and said that it was somewhat dangerous to get in touch with them again because this was what their orders were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Major Boering, when did you leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The town itself I left on the 11th. As you could see on the video, we had quite a lot of transport towards Potocari. All of the population moved in that direction by itself. And once that transport had got going, I myself and my colleague also moved towards Potocari in order to be able to take care of things over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you describe to the Trial Chamber what you saw on your way between Srebrenica and Potocari on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The population actually moving with whatever they could carry in the direction of Potocari. And if they were not capable of walking by themselves, they were carried or moved around in wheelbarrows, or, if possible, in a means of transport belonging to DutchBat itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could you give a rough estimate of how many people dis-located from Srebrenica to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what time of the day was that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in relation to DutchBat and the blocking positions, what happened to those?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The blocking positions were the last, and finally Srebrenica was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, going ahead to Potocari, what did you do once you arrived in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: First of all, I and my colleague reported to Colonel Karremans, and next we started helping to find accommodation for the population that was in the neighbourhood of the compound, to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe the situation as it presented itself to you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Hopeless, lack of food, and extremely uncertain and insecure. At least for the population and for our own battalion, we tried as much as possible to safeguard people and to take medical care of them to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Before moving on, just a last point on this: How was the food and supply situation for DutchBat itself?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: During the preceding months, it had worsened considerably because the convoys were not permitted. So there was hardly any fresh food, and there wasn't any meat either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you explain what you mean by convoys were not permitted?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The convoys always required a clearance from the side of the BSA. And very often, it was not granted or to a limited extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to move on now to the next topic. And that's the Hotel Fontana meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Major Boering, were you called to a meeting at the Hotel Fontana on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, we were invited to attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: By "invited," what do you mean, or who invited you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: We were in touch through a Serbian interpreter there, and he transmitted the message that we were supposed to appear there, at least the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know who told the Serbian interpreter that your presence was requested?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At that point in time, it was unclear. But considering the situation, of course, we complied with that request.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the Serbian interpreter, who did he interpret from, or who was he in contact with?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: He is the interpreter who was employed by the UN. And in practice, he was the interpreter particularly for the Bratunac battalion commander, or the OO. When we got an invitation for the meeting, then at any rate, it came from Mr. Nikolic, or had been ordered by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: At what time was the meeting actually happening?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It took place in the evening at about 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you recall who was present talking first about the Dutch side?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans, and Sergeant-Major Rave, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And from the Bosnian Serb side, who was present?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Present were General Mladic, General Krstic, Colonel Jankovic, Lieutenant-Colonel or Colonel Kosovic, Major Nikolic. Those are the ones I can recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: With your permission, Your Honours, I would like to show him again a brief clip of this first Fontana meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might ask that the Prosecution provide us with an exhibit list of the pieces of evidence they wish to introduce through this witness, like they did yesterday with Mr. Mandzic. We had an exhibit list, so as we went down, we could make notations on whether this is acceptable or not. We haven't received an exhibit list that the Prosecution is using for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's a reasonable request.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I believe we had submitted that document, and we can certainly give you again a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: My apologies to the Court and to the Prosecutor. I was just provided a copy of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You can stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, could you tell to the Trial Chamber who the persons are in this video.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I didn't see anything. On my extreme right, I see a bit of myself; the second one is Sergeant-Major Rave; next in the middle, I see Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans; and to his right and left for me, I see Colonel Jankovic; and in the foreground on the left is General Mladic; and this was in Fontana. That's where the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Major Boering, do you recall what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: What was discussed was the situation of our battalion, what to do with the population, and particularly also the air-raid whereby because of NATO action, people had been killed or injured on the side of the BSA. And General Mladic made it very clear that he was extremely cross about this and that he could, in fact, do with us as he liked. And that's what he wanted to tell us very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You were present at that meeting, Mr. Boering. How did you feel personally at that time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Literally, there was no possibility of negotiating. So there was hardly a possibility for us to change anything about this sorry situation. So I felt extremely limited and restricted. And in the back of my mind, of course, I had -- I was thinking of the population at the compound. It was clear that they did not have enough food and drink to keep it up and to keep going.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I would like to show you another clip. And again the Judges have seen it already, and perhaps you can give us some explanations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think you can stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us who these people are.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, these are the so-called hostage individuals from the observation posts that had been raided during the attack on the enclave. About 30 people. And we had not been in touch with them for at least a week. So when entering this Fontana Hotel, to my right-hand side I saw them sitting in a room. And I went in to talk to them and asked them, past a kind of bodyguard who was there, what their situation was like. And next I reported that to Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans who had already walked on because he was going towards the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How did the meeting end?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: This meeting with General Mladic ended with a clear order by General Mladic for us to make sure that there were representatives from the enclave, if possible, military representatives. And then finally, around 11.00 that evening, we were supposed to return there in order to discuss the situation together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I would like you, because I think I'm still not entirely used to -- sure about Sanction, that you identify on this still picture just again the person you did, and asking you to do that from the left to the right.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: On the left is General Mladic; the second is Colonel Jankovic; next, you have Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans; next is Sergeant-Major Rave; and then there's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Boering. This picture is just a few seconds after the beginning of that videoclip. Now, you just indicated that you needed to make sure that there were representatives from the enclave at a next meeting. Now, did you, in fact, manage to find these representatives?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. Not in the military sense, nor did we find them among the normal civilian administration, but from the local population. We found in the afternoon a former teacher, Mr. Mandzic, whom I was relatively often in touch with. And in my opinion, he was suitable. So that is why we approached him and asked him to come with us. And after a brief while, he was willing, and we prepared him, and then we went to the next meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: By "we prepared him," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Explaining where we were going, what the composition of the previous meeting had been, and what, in our -- our impression was that the intention of the next meeting was going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, you talked about the composition of the previous meeting. And I believe you mentioned a Mr. Krstic or General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall that he was present?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I remember that he was present at one meeting. But right now, I can't recall, but I am certain that he attended one of the meetings, either the next day, and that he was introduced to us as the Drina Corps commander with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, once you had chosen and prepared Mr. Mandzic, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: As agreed, we went to the next meeting together with Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: At what time was that and what location?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That was once again to the same location in Bratunac, around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could show the next clip, I think we should have... If it could be played, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just freeze it for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Major Boering, are you able to identify what this video is about and the persons you --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: This is the meeting that we had then, at 11.00 in the evening in the Fontana Hotel. And if you're asking me to identify the people from left to right, wearing the spectacles on the left is Colonel Jankovic; behind him is General Mladic's bodyguard; seated at the table on the left is the interpreter, Petar; and the next is Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans; and then you see a small part of Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall other people being present which are not on this picture here?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. To the left of Jankovic was General Mladic, and he introduced Colonel Jankovic as his next-in-command to take care of matters if General Mladic were absent, because he might be too busy to take care of matters in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You had mentioned that a Colonel Kosovic or Kosovic was present at the first meeting. Was this person also present at the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, he was present there, too. And he was presented primarily to arrange the transport of the refugees at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall the subject of what was discussed during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: It was mainly about the untenable situation and what solutions would be possible. General Mladic's strong preference to try as much as possible to get the military troops still present in the enclave to surrender and give up their arms, and that anything would be possible as long as they left the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was the atmosphere at the second meeting any different from the previous ones?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, General Mladic was certainly less threatening. It was a normal table set with food, or at least with drink anyway. And Mladic briefly introduced all the operators and described their functions. It was a more formal meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, on the entire video which the Judges have seen, there is at one instance a scream of a pig. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. During the meeting, in any case, to impress us, we heard our type of APCs circling around the building, and we heard that typical pulling noise, and also the squeal of a pig at a certain point. And in some manner, General Mladic indicated that he wanted out of the enclave and that we had to cooperate in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to show you another video still from that meeting. Do you recall this sign board?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At the meeting, General Mladic's bodyguard presented that at the request of General Mladic. It indicates clearly in the Cyrillic alphabet that the former shield positioned on the town hall there needed to be replaced, and that these were old rites that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Major Boering, what do you do after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: After the meeting, we returned. And, well, the idea was to reconvene the next morning. And at that time, we were supposed to go to discuss further details and to try again to locate military BH authorities and to -- for our own leadership to contact the higher level to get directives and to determine positions. And the next morning, we planned to return to the Fontana Hotel. I don't recall exactly, but I believe we even set a time for the next morning. Mr. Mandzic was not entirely comfortable, to put it in English, that he would bear sole responsibility. And for that reason, his delegation was expanded to include two other persons. And they had their own discussions about the course of the subsequent discussions, and at a certain time that was merged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said that you were supposed to bring military persons with you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, we made a limited effort to search for them. But there were serious rumours that the military had left the enclave. And you could tell from the shooting around the enclave and during the second meeting that we had that evening, an actual incident took place in which several Serb military had to leave in a hurry because panic that the Muslim military had broken out of the enclave, to the extent that we could understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is perhaps a good point to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will stop here and continue tomorrow afternoon. Before that -- yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just have one point of clarification. Major Boering keeps referring to the BSA, I believe the BSA is what we call the VRS in all of our documents. Is that the same thing, just for clarification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would like to remind the parties that the Presiding Judge of the Appeals Chamber has made an order rescinding the protective measures concerning this witness. I hope that both parties will get this order and read it because certain materials may be used in the direct examination or cross-examination. Witness, I have to remind you that during your testimony, you are still under the oath. So please do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. We'll see you tomorrow afternoon. The proceedings are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 7.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of July, 2003, at 2.15 p.m.
